one_liner: Fails the quality test (weak financial health, its best days look to be behind it), so price does not matter.

profile.what: The Clorox Company makes cleaning and disinfecting products, bags and wraps, charcoal, cat litter, dressings, water filters and personal-care products. In 2026 it bought the maker of Purell.
profile.money: It sells through grocers, mass retailers, club stores and distributors to institutions. Most sales are in the United States.
profile.valued: Clorox is valued on P/E and dividend yield. The multiple has fallen as sales weakened and debt rose with the acquisition.

summary.sentence: A household-brands owner that has taken on heavy debt as sales soften.
strengths: Gross margin is well above its fiscal 2022 level.
A long record of paying dividends.
Leading brands in most of its categories.
risks: Debt nearly doubled in fiscal 2026 with an acquisition.
Dividends exceeded free cash flow in fiscal 2026.

meaning.what_it_does: Makes household and professional products including Clorox bleach and wipes, Glad bags, Kingsford charcoal, Hidden Valley dressings, Brita filters and Purell sanitiser.
meaning.how_it_makes_money: Sells branded goods to grocers, mass retailers and institutional buyers, mostly in the United States.
meaning.how_it_keeps_making_money: Leading brands in small categories where retailers want only one or two names on the shelf.
meaning.how_it_could_stop: Shoppers switch to store brands, or its newly acquired business fails to justify the debt.

moat.summary: Number-one brands in most of its categories, though many are easy for store brands to copy.

industry.summary: Household products change slowly, though store brands gain ground when budgets are tight.

management.summary: Rebuilt margins after a cyberattack and cost inflation, then borrowed heavily for its largest acquisition.

valuation.method: Fair value is the average of two methods: (1) Owner cash flow: $383M a year: free cash flow less stock-based pay (median of the last three fiscal years and TTM). (2) Damodaran: cash flow to the firm: Sales grow 0–6% for five years, fading to 3%; operating margin held at 13%; cost of capital 7.5%. Cash added, debt subtracted. The owner cash flow method grows the cash for five years, then at half that rate, 3% after year ten, discounted at 10%. Stock-based pay is deducted because it is a real cost to owners.
